subsystems.name: Light absorber
subsystems.role: the layer that swallows sunlight and frees electrons — here built from nanocrystals or electrospun fibres rather than a solid wafer.
parts: colloidal quantum dots or perovskite nanocrystals
absorber film a few hundred nanometres thick

subsystems.name: Charge transport and contacts
subsystems.role: pull electrons and holes apart before they recombine.

subsystems.name: Substrate and encapsulation
subsystems.role: a flexible, very light backing that survives vacuum, ultraviolet light and thermal cycling.

subsystems.name: Cell interconnection
subsystems.role: wires many small cells in series to reach a useful voltage.

subsystems.name: Deployment structure
subsystems.role: folds the blanket for launch and holds it flat once in orbit.

subsystems.name: Power conditioning
subsystems.role: turns the array output into a regulated bus for the spacecraft.

buildSteps.title: Synthesise the nanocrystals
buildSteps.detail: Quantum dots are grown in hot liquid solution so that their size — and therefore the colour of light they absorb — can be tuned precisely. Fibre-based versions are spun from a polymer solution through a charged nozzle.

buildSteps.title: Formulate an ink
buildSteps.detail: The particles are dispersed in a solvent with additives so they can be coated evenly.

buildSteps.title: Deposit the absorber
buildSteps.detail: The ink is spin-coated, slot-die coated or sprayed onto a flexible substrate, or electrospun directly as a mat of nanofibres, then dried.

buildSteps.title: Add transport layers and electrodes
buildSteps.detail: Thin electron- and hole-selecting layers and a transparent contact are deposited on top, often at low temperature to protect the nanocrystals.

buildSteps.title: Pattern and interconnect
buildSteps.detail: Laser scribing or printing divides the film into cells and wires them in series, with bypass diodes so one shaded cell does not kill a string.

buildSteps.title: Encapsulate
buildSteps.detail: Barrier films and edge seals keep out oxygen and water vapour, which currently degrade these materials quickly.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the blanket
buildSteps.detail: Cells are laminated onto a flexible backing and attached to rollable booms or folding panels.

buildSteps.title: Qualify for space
buildSteps.detail: Panels face thermal-vacuum cycling, proton and electron irradiation, vibration and ultraviolet soaking before flight.

buildSteps.title: Integrate with the spacecraft
buildSteps.detail: The array is wired through maximum-power-point trackers to the satellite bus, then deployed and checked in orbit.

prerequisites.why: good films are made in milligram batches in the lab; panels need square metres with uniform particle size.
quantum-dot and perovskite cells lose efficiency quickly in air and under ultraviolet light, and space adds radiation on top.
space arrays already use thin polymer and coverglass laminates that must work with new absorber chemistries.
rollable and folding arrays are flown today, so the mechanical side is largely ready for a new cell type.
converters and trackers exist; they only need matching to the new cells' voltage and current.

pathway.milestone: laboratory quantum-dot and nanofibre cells that beat neither silicon nor multijunction cells in efficiency
pathway.unlocks: understanding of which nanostructures tolerate radiation and ultraviolet light best.

pathway.milestone: pilot coating lines producing square-metre flexible films with multi-year lifetimes
pathway.unlocks: a credible candidate to replace or supplement conventional space cells.

pathway.milestone: flight demonstration on a small satellite, measuring power per kilogram and degradation in real orbit
pathway.unlocks: the data needed for qualification standards.

pathway.milestone: production arrays for satellites and, if launch costs keep falling, very large orbital power platforms
pathway.unlocks: light, cheap, easily deployed power for space habitats and beamed-power concepts.
